two aspects of the photodynamic inactivation of bacterial spores.
the study of the interaction of light and DNA in the presence of oxygen.

the study of the photochemical reactions that take place in the frozen aqueous solution of DNA and the correlation of the results of these studies with the biological effects of ultraviolet irradiation of frozen cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
photoinduced DNA-protein cross-links and bacterial killing at low temperature are correlated, and that thymine dimer formation is not the primary cause of bacterial killing at low temperatures.
the photoinduced DNA-protein cross-links, which are formed in irradiated frozen cells, are the primary cause of the increased killing of bacteria by ultraviolet light at low temperatures.
the photoinduced cross-links between protein and DNA in E. coli are the cause of the increased sensitivity to killing of frozen cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amount of DNA-protein cross-links formed is a better measure of the amount of lethal damage produced by ultraviolet light in frozen E. coli than is the amount of thymine dimer produced.
the killing of bacteria by UV light at low temperature is a function of the amount of DNA cross-linked to protein.
there is no correlation of the amount of thymine dimer with the amount of DNA-protein cross-links, the extent of killing, or the sensitivity of the bacteria to killing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNA-protein cross-links (DPCs) are the primary cause of cell killing at low temperatures.
the sensitivity of cells to killing by ultrviolet irradiation is not a direct function of the amount of thymine dimer formation.
the sensitivity of E. coli to UV irradiation at low temperatures is due primarily to the formation of DNA-protein cross-links.
